channel.title: Science News
channel.description: Aggregated headlines linking to original publishers

item.title: The narwhal’s legendary “unicorn horn” holds a remarkable engineering secret
item.description: The narwhal’s iconic spiral tusk, once prized in Europe as the horn of a mythical unicorn, conceals an extraordinary feat of natural engineering. Using advanced X-ray technology, an international team of scientists discovered that the tusk contains two intertwined microscopic spirals that twist in opposite directions.

item.title: Scientists turn one of the world’s hardest-to-recycle plastics into high-performance lubricating oil
item.description: Virginia Tech scientists have discovered how to transform one of the world's hardest-to-recycle plastics into a valuable ingredient for high-performance engine oil. Their innovative process converts discarded PVC into a useful lubricant material in just three hours. The breakthrough could turn a major source of plastic pollution into a valuable industrial resource while making lubricant production more sustainable.

item.title: Breathing less oxygen tripled lifespan in mice with a deadly brain disorder
item.description: Oxygen is essential for life, but too much of it can become dangerously toxic, particularly in people with certain neurological and mitochondrial disorders. Scientists at Gladstone Institutes have discovered that defective proteins can disrupt the ability of mitochondria to consume oxygen, allowing harmful levels to accumulate in tissues. Remarkably, mice with a genetic disorder that causes motor neuron degeneration lived three times longer when they breathed air containing less oxygen.

item.title: One type of physical activity is linked to a 20% higher dementia risk
item.description: A massive study has revealed that exercising for pleasure and performing physical labor at work may have surprisingly different implications for brain health. While recreational exercise was linked to a 24% lower dementia risk, physically demanding work was associated with a 20% higher risk, suggesting that the context of movement matters.

item.title: Shivelyuch Socked In
item.description: A cloud layer encircled the flanks of the volcano on the Kamchatka Peninsula but left its restless summit caldera in view.

item.title: A fat-burning molecule has an unexpected benefit for your muscles
item.description: Researchers have discovered that a naturally occurring molecule released during exercise helps muscles become stronger, resist fatigue, and withstand damage. The molecule, already available as a dietary supplement, could open new avenues for treating muscle deterioration associated with type 2 diabetes.

item.title: Scientists identify two ages when children may be most vulnerable to screen time
item.description: Scientists have identified two potentially critical periods when screen time may be especially detrimental to children's learning and memory: infancy and the start of formal schooling. Greater screen exposure during these developmental windows was linked to poorer academic performance and weaker working memory years later.

item.title: Harvard’s tiny UV light chip could help shrink quantum computers
item.description: Harvard-led researchers have developed a microscopic device that generates 120 times more ultraviolet light than previous comparable approaches by efficiently converting red light into UV. The breakthrough could unlock smaller quantum computers, ultra-precise atomic clocks, and compact environmental sensors.

item.title: Scientists discover signs of a hidden extinction crisis deep beneath the ocean
item.description: The deep sea has long been considered a safe haven for marine life, but new genetic research suggests a hidden biodiversity crisis may be unfolding far beneath the waves. Scientists analyzing more than a decade of genetic data from five species of deep-sea fish and shrimp in the Gulf discovered troubling signs of extinction risk in every species examined.

item.title: These bizarre prehistoric mammals may have been misunderstood for 150 years
item.description: Giant horned mammals that emerged shortly after the extinction of the dinosaurs may have had far fewer physical differences between males and females than scientists once believed. The discovery challenges a classic example of sexual dimorphism and raises questions about how historical biases have shaped our understanding of extinct animals.

item.title: The haunting loveliness of boglands: Books in brief
item.description: Nature, Published online: 27 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03885-4 Andrew Robinson reviews five of the best science picks.

item.title: Brain area’s mysterious role in speech decoded at last
item.description: Nature, Published online: 27 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03800-x Wernicke’s area is known for processing spoken words, but brain recordings reveal that it also makes a crucial contribution to a related cognitive task.

item.title: Life-saving cancer drug pumped out by a plant
item.description: Nature, Published online: 27 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03801-w In a proof-of-concept study, scientists have coaxed a tobacco-related plant to synthesize the chemotherapy drug paclitaxel.

item.title: Postcards from your graves
item.description: Nature, Published online: 27 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03523-z A disastrous outcome.

item.title: Why the incoming US Congress should ban the development of self-improving AI
item.description: Nature, Published online: 27 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03849-8 Voters are demanding greater control over this new technology. Political leaders must respond by keeping humans in charge of AI development.

item.title: This dietary supplement may have an unexpected benefit for the brain
item.description: A naturally derived dietary supplement called urolithin A may help the brain get more oxygen and nutrients when it needs them most. In a randomized clinical trial involving 50 middle-aged adults with obesity, researchers found that taking the supplement daily for four weeks increased blood flow to the brain during a challenging memory task, particularly in a region involved in working memory.

item.title: For decades, scientists may have misunderstood how brain cells work
item.description: A major new study challenges a long-standing assumption about how the brain works, revealing that most neurons are versatile multitaskers rather than highly specialized workers. By analyzing recordings from 43 regions of the mouse brain, researchers discovered that although some neurons are dedicated to specific functions, most respond to a wide variety of information in remarkably distinct ways.

item.title: Common supplements rival antibiotics in treating severe gum disease
item.description: A combination of omega-3 and low-dose aspirin produced results comparable to antibiotics when used alongside standard treatment for severe gum disease, with benefits persisting long after supplementation ended. The surprising discovery could offer an alternative for some patients while reducing reliance on antibiotics.

item.title: Loneliness is making us sick, but we may be treating it all wrong
item.description: Loneliness can be surprisingly deadly, with previous research linking it to a roughly 30% increase in the risk of premature death. However, a new study warns that treating loneliness as a medical condition could distract from its deeper social causes. While healthcare professionals can offer support, lasting solutions may require rebuilding communities and fundamentally changing the way people live and work.

item.title: The surprising reason women seem better at multitasking than men
item.description: Men and women appear to be similarly capable of multitasking, but men are more than twice as likely to ignore conversation while juggling multiple activities. Researchers believe this unexpected difference may help explain why women are widely perceived as better multitaskers.

item.title: Deep beneath Australia, hidden caves could unlock the secrets of alien worlds
item.description: Scientists have solved the mystery of strange trenches scattered across Australia’s vast Nullarbor Plain, revealing an extensive hidden world beneath the surface. These subtle landscape features are created as deeply buried cave systems slowly collapse upward over millions of years. The discovery could help researchers locate unexplored caves containing ancient environmental records and unusual life forms.

item.title: This 345-million-year-old fossil had scientists fooled for decades
item.description: A famous 345-million-year-old fossil has turned out to be something entirely different from what scientists believed for decades. Advanced X-ray imaging revealed hidden gills and thousands of tiny teeth, exposing a primitive aquatic or amphibious creature rather than an early reptile. The discovery suggests that several adaptations associated with life on land actually evolved in animals still dependent on water.

item.title: Seeking Refuge on Resolution Island
item.description: New Zealanders have long envisioned the island as a predator-free zone for native birds, but swimming stoats have shown a resolve of their own.

item.title: Too much of this common nutrient could be accelerating blood vessel aging
item.description: Researchers have uncovered a kidney protein that may hold an important key to vascular aging and longevity. The protein helps prevent excess phosphate from accumulating in the blood and gradually turning flexible blood vessels rigid. In animal models, a deficiency accelerated blood vessel aging and significantly shortened lifespan, while reducing dietary phosphate helped lessen the damage.

item.title: Scientists discover mysterious lakes more than a mile beneath the Red Sea
item.description: More than a mile beneath the surface of the Red Sea, scientists have discovered rare underwater lakes that could reveal secrets about Earth's ancient oceans and the possibility of alien life. Known as brine pools, these extremely salty, oxygen-free environments are surprisingly teeming with microbial life, challenging our understanding of where living organisms can survive.

item.title: Astronomers may have discovered a black hole born before the first stars
item.description: A mysterious object named Phoebe, detected when it briefly magnified a distant star, could be a primordial black hole formed just after the Big Bang. With an estimated mass only three times that of the Moon, it may be a 13-billion-year-old cosmic relic that offers new clues to the mystery of dark matter.

item.title: World’s largest trial of robotic knee replacement reveals surprising results
item.description: Robot-assisted knee replacement surgery offers greater surgical precision, but a landmark clinical trial has revealed a surprising limitation. Despite the advanced technology, patients experienced no meaningful improvements in pain, mobility, or recovery compared with conventional surgery after one year.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 26 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03874-7 A system tested in mice mimics a protein that declines with age and could help to improve fertility treatments in future.

item.title: Navigating grief in academia: ways to find balance
item.description: Nature, Published online: 26 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02752-6 Pamela Yeh found it hard to manage grief and the demands of her work. Here are some steps that helped her to ease the burden.

item.title: Has AI just cracked Internet encryption? Rumoured ‘bombshell’ stuns scientists
item.description: Nature, Published online: 26 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03875-6 AI-generated algorithms could be about to break public-key cryptography, the technology central to commerce, banking and privacy.

item.title: Orangutans face bleak future after Indonesia’s devastating wildfires
item.description: Nature, Published online: 26 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03828-z The super El Niño intensified Indonesian fires, which ravaged the habitat of the critically endangered Bornean orangutan.

item.title: Daily briefing: A guide to the Riemann hypothesis
item.description: Nature, Published online: 26 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03894-3 Get to grips with the famed conjecture, and hear mathematicians’ reactions to its proofs. Plus, the benefits of eating with other people.

item.title: Scientists discover a surprising twist in how the body burns calories
item.description: Researchers have discovered that a drug can significantly increase the body's energy expenditure without clearly activating calorie-burning brown fat. The unexpected finding reveals a new challenge in developing obesity treatments that harness the body's natural fat-burning machinery.

item.title: NASA Enhances Supplier Program, Announces Mentor-Protégé Agreement
item.description: How NASA works with small businesses is evolving, and as a result, the agency is strengthening the domestic aerospace industrial base to support future exploration missions through its recently renamed Small Business Supplier Development Program. As part of the program, NASA announced its latest Mentor-Protégé Agreement, this one signed between The Boeing Company and GRACE […]

item.title: NASA Eyes Crop Candidates for Future Menus
item.description: As NASA prepares for future missions to the Moon and Mars, researchers are studying crops that could provide astronauts with fresh food, nutrition, and variety far from Earth. Such crop variety can help with menus in deep space, something top of mind this week as the nation celebrates Thanksgiving. Recent testing points to strawberries, […]

item.title: Childhood, Career Come Full Circle for Budget Analyst at NASA Goddard
item.description: Conversations about NASA were the norm around the dinner table during Ashley Knight’s childhood. Her parents worked at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, and discussions about happenings at the agency continued even when they came home from the office. “I remember a poignant dialogue we had after the space shuttle Challenger disaster,” […]

item.title: Eye of the Sahara
item.description: The Richat Structure, also known as the “Eye of the Sahara,” is seen from the International Space Station as it orbited above on Nov. 14, 2026. It is an eroded geological dome about 100 million years old created by igneous activity and uplift in the nation of Mauritania. In this type of geologic structure, rocks […]

item.title: NASA’s Hubble Views Ocean of Stars in Groundwork for Roman
item.description: These Hubble observations are part of a survey that will help researchers better interpret upcoming Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope observations as they seek to characterize the stars and search for exoplanets in this busy region of our galaxy.

item.title: Common sleep and anxiety drugs could be harming aging brains
item.description: Nearly one in three older adults with dementia or other cognitive disorders takes potentially harmful medications that can worsen brain function and increase the risk of hospitalization and premature death. Despite encouraging progress over the past decade, researchers warn that medication-related harm remains a major and potentially preventable threat to healthy aging.

item.title: Peppermint oil significantly lowers blood pressure in just 20 days
item.description: Peppermint oil may have a surprisingly powerful effect on blood pressure. In a randomized study of 40 adults, researchers found that taking small doses twice daily for 20 days lowered systolic blood pressure by an average of 8.5 mmHg. Those receiving a placebo experienced no significant improvement. The discovery points to a promising, low-cost natural approach to managing mildly elevated blood pressure.

item.title: A space telescope hunting for dark matter just discovered something unexpected
item.description: ESA’s Euclid space telescope has discovered its first previously unknown comet, despite being designed to study distant galaxies and the mysteries of the dark Universe. The icy object is approximately 1.3 billion kilometers from Earth and follows an unusual orbit that takes thousands of years to complete.

item.title: Physicists trap antimatter in a breakthrough that could explain why the universe exists
item.description: Positrons are the antimatter counterpart of an electron. Physicists trapped a positron and cooled it to temperatures near absolute zero. Positron is suspended in a wall-free trap, safely separated from ordinary matter. Team will conduct most precise comparison yet between matter and antimatter. Any difference between the electron and positron could expose cracks in the Standard Model of particle physics.

item.title: A tiny injectable sensor could change how millions of people monitor blood sugar
item.description: Texas A&M researchers have discovered a way to dramatically reduce the cost of a key component in an experimental injectable glucose sensor without sacrificing performance. The technology uses fluorescent light to measure glucose levels from beneath the skin.

item.title: What is a thought made of? Why human consciousness may be beyond AI’s reach
item.description: A new theory suggests that the brain may chemically encode and retrieve memories rather than relying solely on electrical signals. Researchers propose that interactions between brain cells and their molecular surroundings could help explain the intimate connection between memory, emotion, and thought. Their findings challenge the assumption that increasingly powerful computers could eventually develop human-like consciousness.

item.title: Stanford scientists discover 3 hidden brain types behind ADHD and anxiety
item.description: An AI-powered analysis of thousands of children's brain scans has revealed three distinct brain types underlying ADHD and anxiety that do not neatly fit traditional diagnoses. These hidden biological patterns can appear before a diagnosis is made, potentially enabling earlier detection and more effective, personalized treatments.

item.title: Physicists just sent an unblockable message through a brick wall using gravity
item.description: Scientists have successfully transmitted a message through a brick wall using nothing but gravity, an old elevator, and an incredibly sensitive detector. By moving a massive counterweight between two positions, researchers encoded the word "Gravity" into tiny changes in gravitational pull. Unlike Wi-Fi or radio signals, gravity passes through ordinary barriers without being blocked, offering a potentially revolutionary way to communicate.

item.title: Einstein’s 120-year-old theory may be missing something big about the Big Bang
item.description: A surprising discovery by MIT and UC Santa Barbara physicists reveals that Einstein’s famous theory of particle motion misses something important when particles travel near the speed of light. Their new calculations show that heavy quarks moving through an ultra-hot plasma experience rare but unusually powerful jolts that Einstein’s traditional model cannot fully explain.

item.title: Scientists discover a hidden gut defense that could prevent colon cancer
item.description: A common antibody in the gut may be a powerful natural defense against colon cancer, with researchers finding that mice lacking it developed more than twice as many tumors. Restoring the antibody eliminated the increased risk, revealing a promising new avenue for preventing cancer before it starts.

item.title: The leading cities in the world for high-quality research in 2025

item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03472-7 The city-state’s compact size and centralized governance allow digital infrastructure to be introduced with unusual speed and consistency.

item.title: How arteries keep their shape in the face of overgrowth-inducing mutations
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03491-4 Why do cancer-associated mutations cause some blood vessels to develop abnormally, but not arteries? The answer lies in the identity and maturity of the affected cells.

item.title: What is the Riemann hypothesis? A guide to the famed conjecture that rules prime numbers
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03854-x The biggest problem in mathematics has to do with a statistical test familiar to scientists.

item.title: Saving Nepal’s wild orchids — in photos
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03475-4 Prized for their ornamental and medicinal value, hundreds of orchids are illegally harvested and sold each year. Now, conservationist Reshu Bashyal is leading an effort to protect them.

item.title: A fine-grained reconstruction of barley’s evolutionary history
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03494-1 Chromosome-scale genome sequences from across the barley genus Hordeum reveal large structural variation, evidence of ancient genetic exchange and extensive divergence of regulatory sequences. These evolutionary processes have generated diversity that could be used to improve cultivated barley.

item.title: A powerful HIV vaccine is finally within reach — thanks to these super antibodies
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03718-4 Potent immune responses against diverse HIV strains have ignited the field, but major hurdles remain.

item.title: Can Beijing scale up its smart-city ambitions?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03470-9 The world’s leading science city is testing AI and intelligent transport at scale, but linking data across its innovation hubs remains a challenge.

item.title: From sketch to publication-ready flowchart: how AI tools can bridge the gap
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03513-1 The use of generative AI is a practical way to translate hand-drawn scientific diagrams into digital formats without handing over total control, explains Ensar Aydemir.

item.title: The world’s leading science cities are changing — here’s why
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03466-5 Nature Index data reveal the cities that are gaining ground in research, as smart technologies transform how urban centres operate and compete for talent.

item.title: Gut microbes can adapt to our ageing bodies
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03268-9 A study of more than 10,000 individuals reveals specific mutations in gut bacteria that arise during human ageing, but few mutations associated with disease.

item.title: China’s AI-powered smart-city model is going global
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03473-6 China is using AI and big data to connect its cities and rural regions. Now, its smart-city technologies are attracting international interest.

item.title: Pockets in compacted DNA tune gene activation
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03492-3 The stochastic activation of specific genes is needed for the proper formation of neuronal circuits. Opposing forces act on inactive DNA to balance this process.

item.title: Helsinki puts trust at the heart of its smart-city model
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03469-2 Open urban data, recycled data-centre heat and a public AI register are helping the Finnish capital develop responsible urban technology.

item.title: London’s people-first approach to smart-city development
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03471-8 Digital twins and open-data platforms are part of London’s aim to innovate for citizens.

item.title: Bogong moths can migrate using an internal geomagnetic compass
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03693-w Australian migratory moths navigate long distances, in part owing to a stellar ‘compass’. It transpires that they have another compass that detects the inclination, or angle, of Earth’s magnetic field lines and that probably relies on a light-dependent quantum-mechanical mechanism similar to the one found in night-migratory songbirds.

item.title: Can smart cities attract the talent they need to thrive?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03467-4 The challenges of high-tech cities in South Korea and China reveal what scientists really want.

item.title: Dengue has exploded globally with shocking speed
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03813-6 The number of recorded cases of the mosquito-borne disease worldwide rose by a factor of 34 over 34 years.

item.title: The Mona Lisa Lottery
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03521-1 Worth the wait.

item.title: The world has a golden chance to improve HIV prevention: don’t squander it
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03809-2 Generic versions of an effective HIV drug have been approved, and an HIV vaccine is on the horizon. Now is no time for funders to take their foot off the pedal.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03474-5 A description of the terminology and methodology used in this supplement, and a guide to the functionality that is available free online at natureindex.com.

item.title: Succumbing to certainty is a failure in science
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03837-y Researchers can face pressure from policymakers and politicians to provide single, definitive answers to complex challenges. They should resist, says Andy Stirling.

item.title: Rare gene variants can affect a person’s height by up to 17 centimetres
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03872-9 An analysis of 1.4 million people uncovered rare gene variants that are helping to unpick the genetic architecture behind the heritability of height.

item.title: Enzymatic reactions adapted to make ‘living’ chains of sugars
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03382-8 By tuning the binding between enzymes that chain sugars together and the molecules that initiate the reaction, precise chain lengths have been made for biological studies.

item.title: ‘If we can solve Riemann, what can’t we do?’: mathematicians shocked and excited by AI breakthroughs
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03835-0 Awe, anxiety and opportunity: mathematics community shares mixed emotions following the solution of the field’s biggest unsolved problem.

item.title: Just eight universities dominate Nobel and other top economics prizes
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03333-3 Economics is the outlier — top prizes in science, engineering and other social sciences go to researchers at a greater variety of institutions.

item.title: An enduring climatic burden from past peatland drainage
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11339-0 Reconstruction of radiative forcing resulting from worldwide peatland drainage over the past two centuries reveals a persistent net warming effect caused by the dominant forcing of drainage-induced CO2 emissions over that of avoided CH4 emissions.

item.title: Single-cell variant-to-enhancer-to-gene map for coronary artery disease
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11275-z A multi-omic gene-expression and chromatin-accessibility map of human coronary artery disease provides a framework for mapping disease-associated genetic variants to cell types, chromatin states and gene programmes in human disease.

item.title: Heterogeneity co-evolves with architecture to determine colon cancer outcome
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11301-0 Architectural interfaces in colorectal cancer drive cell state diversification through mechanochemical reprogramming of stem cell identities.

item.title: A gut–brain sensory-motor circuit regulates sugar ingestion in Drosophila
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11315-8 In flies, sugar-sensing enteric neurons activate brain neurons that inhibit crop duct motor neurons, relaxing the foregut muscles to facilitate food transfer to the crop, which sustains ingestion and regulates food intake.

item.title: Quantum-enhanced sensing with 500 photons via Fock-space confocal focusing
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11353-2 Quantum confocal microscopy enables deterministic preparation of high-photon-number Fock-like states with up to 500 photons, reducing photon-number variance by 21.5 dB and achieving record displacement-sensing precision 19.2 dB beyond the standard quantum limit.

item.title: Licensing mechanisms during RNA-guided DNA integration by type I-F3 CAST
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11287-9 RNA-guided DNA integration by type I-F3 CRISPR-associated transposases (CASTs) is enhanced by redesigned TnsA and a holo complex whose coordinated conformational licensing reveals a conserved mechanistic framework for engineering highly active CASTs.

item.title: Middle–Late Pleistocene Denisovans and unresolved Homo in southern China
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11341-6 Dental morphology and proteomic analyses of fossils from southern China identify lineages with and without Denisovan affinity, indicating the diversity of hominin populations in this region in the Middle to Late Pleistocene.

item.title: Sustainable cement production via a liquid-phase pathway
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11313-w Sustainable cement production can be achieved by accelerating its reaction kinetics through a microwave carbon-plasma method, reducing the standard processing time from hours to seconds.

item.title: Context-dependent response of endothelial cells to PIK3CA mutation
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11318-5 Expression of PIK3CAH1047R in arterial precursors disrupts arterial differentiation and promotes the acquisition of venous features.

item.title: Augmenting reality with integrated photonics
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11146-7 Integrated photonics could overcome key size, power and performance trade-offs in augmented-reality glasses, enabling compact, efficient displays while opening opportunities across quantum computing, bioimaging and optical sensing.

item.title: Enzymatic living polymerization for polysaccharide synthesis
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11304-x An enzymatic method for making high-molecular-weight polysaccharides in a way similar to synthetic polymerization techniques, rather than biosynthetically, is presented.

item.title: Coherent parity oscillations in coupled minimal Kitaev chains
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11309-6 Coherent time-resolved rotations between parity states encoded by four poor man’s Majoranas are demonstrated in two coupled minimal Kitaev chains, providing a foundation for topologically protected qubits in longer chains.

item.title: Transcription from megabase-scale heterochromatin generates neural barcodes
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11311-y Interrogation of the clustered protocadherin locus shows an unexpected ability of genes to transcribe within a seemingly silent chromatin environment.

item.title: Structural basis of RNA-guided DNA integration by type I CAST systems
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11196-x Structural analyses reveal the mechanism underlying RNA-guided DNA integration by type I CRISPR-associated transposases (CASTs) and provide a framework for developing CASTs into site-specific genome-editing tools.

item.title: Clinical landscape of cardiometabolic heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11231-x This Review covers the current state of research into heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) from a variety of perspectives, focusing on the clinical context.

item.title: An extremophile transgene improves drought resistance and yield in cereals
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11151-w The use of an extremophile fungus-derived gene decouples the trade-off of drought stress and reduced crop yield by boosting drought resilience and increasing yields in wheat, rice and maize.

item.title: Disturbances and climate drive tree elevational shifts
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11354-1 Climate change and natural disturbances are key drivers of tree abundance dynamics: warming tends to shift tree abundance upslope whereas major disturbances, such as wildfires and insect outbreaks, tend to shift it downslope, creating opposing pressures on tree species’ elevational redistribution.

item.title: Unconventional resistivity reduction in NbP semimetal nanoribbons
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11288-8 Niobium phosphide semimetal nanoribbons show decreasing resistivity with decreasing width, unlike the classical behaviour of metals such as copper, offering a platform for nanoscale wires and interconnects via industry-friendly top-down nanofabrication.

item.title: De novo design of high-potency dual-target therapeutic peptides with ORIDTP
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11338-1 The artificial intelligence platform ORIDTP enabled de novo design of potent dual-target therapeutic peptides, generating candidate anti-obesity, antidiabetic and anticancer peptides with strong in vivo efficacy and broad cross-target generalizability.

item.title: Engineering signalling centres to trigger human trunk morphogenesis in vitro
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11326-5 A high-throughput synthetic embryology platform reveals how transient spatial cues establish two self-sustaining signalling centres that organize trunk-like morphogenesis, enabling the study of early human development and congenital disorders.

item.title: Rare-variant genetic architecture of height in over 1.4 million individuals
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11345-2 Analysis of exomes from over 1.4 million participants implicates 207 genes, including large effect coding variants and gene burden tests, and demonstrates the utility of large-scale sequencing for trait prediction and variant interpretation.

item.title: Submillimetre hot-electron transport in manganese-doped quantum dot solids
item.description: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11279-9 A phototransport regime driven by spin exchange is demonstrated in manganese-doped quantum dot solids, enabling the generation, long-range transport and regeneration of hot carriers and yielding submillimetre drift lengths.

item.title: New nose drops restore youthful memory and fight Alzheimer’s in aging mice
item.description: A revolutionary new nasal treatment has restored youthful learning and memory performance in aging mice while preventing severe cognitive decline in mice with Alzheimer’s-like disease. Developed using technology similar to COVID-19 mRNA vaccines, the nose drops stimulate production of a brain-protecting protein that strengthens neurons and supports memory. Remarkably, the treatment preserved brain function without removing Alzheimer’s-associated plaques, suggesting a completely different way to combat cognitive decline.

item.title: A black hole the size of an atom could destroy an entire star
item.description: MIT scientists have discovered that tiny black holes left over from the Big Bang could slowly devour stars from within, eventually triggering spectacular explosions visible across galaxies. Detecting these unusual cosmic events could reveal the existence of primordial black holes and help solve the mystery of dark matter.

item.title: A simple metal is hiding a strange new form of magnetism
item.description: Scientists have discovered a strange form of magnetism in an ordinary-looking metal that has no overall magnetization yet profoundly changes how electrons behave. The breakthrough offers a promising new path toward understanding exotic quantum materials and developing future electronic technologies.

item.title: 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals an ingenious waterproofing trick
item.description: A 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck has revealed sophisticated waterproofing techniques involving pine tar and beeswax. Microscopic pollen grains trapped in the ancient coatings are now helping scientists reconstruct where the vessel may have traveled and undergone repairs more than two millennia ago.

item.title: Cannabis users develop psychosis years earlier, and the gap grows with age
item.description: A major analysis of 149 studies found that cannabis users develop psychosis an average of 2.5 years earlier than non-users, with the difference growing to more than six years among adults 30 and older. Researchers warn that cannabis-related psychiatric risks may accumulate over time, challenging the belief that using marijuana after adolescence is relatively safe.

item.title: Scientists discover a new type of depression that common antidepressants struggle to treat
item.description: Researchers have discovered a new subtype of depression that may affect nearly one in four people with severe, recurrent, or persistent depression. Known as "circadian depression," it is linked to the body's internal clock and is associated with night owl tendencies, excessive sleep, persistent exhaustion, and more severe symptoms. Traditional antidepressants often work less effectively for these individuals, potentially explaining why some people struggle to find relief.

item.title: Ancient rocks from the Moon’s far side rewrite the Solar System’s violent past
item.description: Scientists studying ancient rocks from the Moon’s far side have uncovered surprising evidence that challenges decades of thinking about the Solar System’s violent past. Instead of a single catastrophic bombardment, asteroid impacts appear to have declined gradually over billions of years, revealing new clues about Earth's early evolution and the origins of life.

item.title: Earth's next ice age may have already begun. Global warming stopped it
item.description: Scientists have uncovered surprising evidence that Earth’s next ice age may have already begun, only to be stopped by global warming. By studying ancient plants preserved beneath the Barnes Ice Cap in the Canadian Arctic, researchers discovered that the remnants of a massive ice sheet began expanding again about 2,000 years ago, signaling the possible start of a new glacial period. But by the 1960s, rising temperatures had reversed that growth, causing the ice to shrink instead.

item.title: IBM quantum computer solves problem classical computers can’t in just 15 minutes
item.description: IBM and University of Chicago researchers have demonstrated that a quantum computer can complete an extraordinarily complex calculation in just 15 minutes, beyond the practical reach of leading classical computing methods. A novel error-detection technique also allows scientists to establish confidence in the accuracy of the results, overcoming a major hurdle in quantum computing.

item.title: America is building just 10% of the power lines it needs, experts warn
item.description: America’s power grid is falling dangerously behind as electricity demand skyrockets, fueled by data centers, electric vehicles, and industry. The U.S. is building only 10% of the new high-voltage transmission lines experts say it needs, threatening higher energy prices and greater blackout risks. Researchers argue that political obstacles and outdated regulations, rather than technological limitations, are the real problem.

item.title: Earth’s ancient oceans may have fooled scientists about its oxygen history
item.description: Earth’s journey from an oxygen-starved world to a planet capable of supporting complex life may have unfolded very differently than scientists once believed. A new analysis suggests that oxygen accumulated in the atmosphere in three major stages, with the oceans taking millions or even hundreds of millions of years to catch up.

item.title: Depression may be an early warning sign of Alzheimer's disease
item.description: Depression in older adults may be more than a mental health concern. Scientists discovered that accumulating tau protein, a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease, was linked to worsening depressive symptoms in people who still had normal memory and thinking abilities. The faster tau built up in the brain, the faster depressive symptoms increased, suggesting that mood changes could emerge before cognitive decline.

item.title: Strange new materials can crawl, walk, and dig like living creatures
item.description: Scientists have developed remarkable materials that can crawl, walk, and dig using their own internal energy, potentially paving the way for a new generation of autonomous soft robots. They also discovered that making individual components more active can paradoxically make the entire material less responsive, challenging a long-standing principle of engineering.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 24 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03821-6 Large post-mortem study identifies epigenetic changes in the brain linked to post-traumatic stress disorder.

item.title: Pakistani astronaut to become first foreign visitor to China’s space station
item.description: Nature, Published online: 24 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03829-y Muhammad Zeeshan Ali is flying this week to the Tiangong module aboard a Chinese spacecraft.

item.title: Watch out, AlphaFold: Claude and ChatGPT’s new biology skills wow scientists
item.description: Nature, Published online: 24 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03836-z Anthropic and OpenAI’s language models can design proteins and predict their sequences and structures — capabilities previously displayed only by specialized AI tools.

item.title: How acidic compounds in human sweat open a mosquito ion channel
item.description: Nature, Published online: 24 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03381-9 Structures of a mosquito receptor bound to acids from human skin could inspire tactics to stifle the attraction of malaria-carrying mosquitoes to humans.

item.title: Blend public cash and private innovation to unlock drug development
item.description: Nature, Published online: 24 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03723-7 Common health conditions lack medicines and treatments because industry finds them too risky to invest in. Here’s what would help.

item.title: Daily briefing: Is AI ‘the end of mathematics as we know it’?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 24 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03841-2 Mathematicians are grappling with the future of their field in the age of AI. Plus, trauma leaves molecular scars in brain cells and whether scientists are responsible for their tooting their own horns.

item.title: ‘The worst COP ever’ offers a chance to learn from failure
item.description: Nature, Published online: 24 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03810-9 COP31 ended without agreement, but consensus-based approaches are essential to solve global issues, and ‘failures’ can lead to decisive action at future talks.

item.title: AI is ‘the end of mathematics as we know it’ — where does the field go next?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 24 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03719-3 Mathematicians are bracing for a future when their profession could be mostly delegated to machines.

item.title: Menopause can speed up brain ageing — hormone therapy might protect it
item.description: Nature, Published online: 24 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03667-y Studies are revealing how menopause can also affect the progression of Alzheimer’s disease.

item.title: New gum disease treatment kills bad bacteria while sparing the good
item.description: Researchers in Japan have developed an innovative gum disease treatment that uses egg yolk antibodies and near-infrared light to destroy harmful bacteria without harming beneficial microbes. Unlike conventional treatments, the approach preserves the mouth's natural bacterial balance and protects healthy gum cells. In mice, it significantly reduced the bone loss associated with periodontitis, a major cause of tooth loss.

item.title: A galactic shock wave could rewrite the map of the Milky Way
item.description: A surprising discovery suggests the Milky Way may be making stars in places where most galaxies cannot. Scientists found evidence that a massive rotating structure near the galactic center is creating powerful shock waves that trigger star formation rather than suppress it. Even more unexpectedly, part of the Norma spiral arm may not be a spiral arm at all, but a vast region where new stars are being born.

item.title: Two monster black holes from the dawn of time defy explanation
item.description: Astronomers have discovered the oldest known compact pair of quasars, powered by two enormous black holes that existed just 900 million years after the Big Bang. Weighing an astonishing 1.5 billion and 400 million times the mass of the Sun, these cosmic giants somehow grew to incredible sizes far earlier than current theories can explain.

item.title: Mysterious new viruses reveal a missing link in evolution
item.description: Scientists have discovered previously unknown viruses that could help explain how some of life’s earliest biological structures evolved. The surprising findings challenge a longstanding evolutionary theory and suggest that viruses may have hidden capabilities far beyond simply infecting cells.

item.title: Scientists discover that leukemia can begin developing 50 years before diagnosis
item.description: A groundbreaking study reveals that acute myeloid leukemia (AML), an aggressive blood cancer, can begin developing more than 50 years before diagnosis, with the first cancer-driving mutation appearing before age 20 in two-thirds of cases. Scientists discovered that these mutated cells grow in surprisingly predictable patterns, accelerating dramatically as additional mutations accumulate.

item.title: Earth's core may be leaking a 4.5-billion-year-old secret
item.description: Scientists have discovered an unusual carbon signature in Hawaiian volcanic rocks that suggests some of Earth's carbon originated in ancient meteorites and later escaped from deep within the planet's core. The discovery raises an astonishing possibility: Carbon essential to life may have traveled from space to Earth's depths before emerging through volcanoes billions of years later.

item.title: Archaeologists reveal a powerful Iron Age king may have been a woman
item.description: Archaeologists have uncovered evidence that Verica, the Iron Age ruler whose exile helped trigger Rome’s invasion of Britain in AD 43, was actually a woman. The discovery challenges centuries of historical assumptions and suggests that a largely forgotten female leader may have changed the course of British history.

item.title: This tiny spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome 50% larger than a human’s
item.description: A tiny California trapdoor spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome roughly 50% larger than a human's, despite being only about the size of a quarter. Scientists discovered that its enormous genome contains 4.6 billion DNA base pairs and 52 chromosomes, revealing surprising clues about spider evolution.

item.title: Mice slept 70% less after scientists switched off these brain cells
item.description: Scientists have discovered brain cells that actively generate the irresistible urge to sleep, and shutting them down allowed mice to sleep 70% less than normal. Remarkably, many of the animals avoided the severe behavioral consequences of sleep deprivation, raising intriguing possibilities for future sleep research.

item.title: U.S. loses measles elimination status after 25 years as vaccine myths persist
item.description: The United States has lost its measles elimination status after more than 25 years, and a new survey reveals widespread misconceptions about the deadly disease and its vaccine. With measles cases surging, more than one-third of Americans still believe or are uncertain about the debunked vaccine-autism link, while most don't know the disease's risks or how many vaccine doses children need.

item.title: Scientists discover a surprising link between weak bones and faster brain aging
item.description: Weakening bones may reveal more about brain health than scientists previously realized, with new research linking lower spinal bone density to faster cognitive decline and accelerated changes in the brain's white matter. The surprising connection suggests that routine medical scans could help uncover hidden warning signs of brain aging and identify people at increased risk of dementia.

item.title: Type 2 diabetes linked to 53% higher Alzheimer’s risk, major review finds
item.description: People with type 2 diabetes face a 53% higher risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease, according to a major new review of 40 studies. Researchers estimate that nearly five out of every 1,000 people with type 2 diabetes develop Alzheimer’s each year. By focusing specifically on these two conditions, the study offers a clearer understanding of a potentially serious connection between metabolic health and brain health.

item.title: A mysterious gap hints at black holes born from stars that never exploded
item.description: Massive stars may be quietly collapsing into black holes without ever producing the spectacular supernova explosions scientists typically expect. A surprising pattern in 257 black hole mergers suggests these mysterious stellar disappearances could explain the origins of a large population of black holes throughout the universe.

item.title: DNA’s secret sunscreen may have helped life survive on early Earth
item.description: Scientists have uncovered a surprising reason why early life may have survived Earth's intense ultraviolet radiation: a key component of DNA appears to turn potentially destructive damage into something easier to repair. The discovery could help solve a decades-old evolutionary mystery and reveal how life endured the harsh conditions of our planet's earliest days.

item.title: A 194-year-old tortoise has a remarkable anti-aging secret hidden in its DNA
item.description: At an astonishing 194 years old, Jonathan the giant tortoise is the world's oldest living land animal, and scientists may have finally uncovered the secrets behind his extraordinary lifespan. Researchers identified 287 unique genetic variants linked to processes that help repair damaged DNA, control inflammation, regulate insulin, and suppress cancer.

item.title: AI may not work like the human brain after all, scientists discover
item.description: AI may not think like the human brain after all, according to a striking new discovery that challenges how scientists understand artificial intelligence. Researchers found that even AI models that closely predict brain activity may rely on internal processes the brain doesn't use, raising important questions about their reliability in neuroscience research.
